n_TOF↔DREAM matching failures: root cause found, data recoverable

Overnight 2026-08-11 → 08-12. Two Claude sessions working adversarially (this one + the matching-QA/campaign session), ~20 measurements, 12 wrong models killed. Full campaign record: ntof_processing/SLIM_CAMPAIGN_2026-08-12.md.

Verdict: the slim pipeline is healthy — but 25.7 % of attempted beam pulses have no n_TOF match (51,331 of ~200k pulses; 107 of 291 segments; six DREAM runs completely dark), and none of it is bad data. The DREAM detector, DAQ and beam are all exonerated by direct measurement.

Cause: pulse_match.match_subrun's count-only wall-clock alignment is degenerate under the accelerator supercycle (the recorded-bunch pattern repeats every 39.6 s / 43.2 s depending on the hour), ties between the true lock and a supercycle-shifted one, silently breaks the tie toward the more negative offset, and reports perfect match statistics either way.

Recovery is demonstrated, not hypothetical: a formerly total-loss hour (run_96/0001 × 224597) re-joined with the measured +26-bunch shift runs through the unmodified standard chain at 95.47 % efficiency, 0.065 % accidentals — statistically indistinguishable from the healthy fleet.

Update, 08-12 morning — the fix is implemented and committed (ce8ced7): lock enumeration + intensity-fluctuation arbitration + loud failure on ambiguity, provenance in every product. Acceptance: the same lost hour now slims end-to-end with zero manual input at 95.4773 %. The whole-hour class (41 segments) recovers by plain re-run.

Update, 08-12 midday — there were TWO bugs, and the second one was also ours (3a6c284). The "sliver class" was blamed here on an n_TOF-side time-base anomaly. That was wrong. It is a one-line defect in our own bunch_join: the offset bootstrap took its median over all bursts including those with no pulse in the run at all, which on a boundary sliver is the majority, walking the offset off a lock the scan had already found correctly. The exemplar that had defeated every probe now fits at 95.56 %. Details in the section below. Both bugs destroy data rather than corrupting it — a wrongly-joined segment finds no coincidence, fails its clock fit and writes no file — so every product already shipped is sound.

How it presented

The 2026-08-11 re-slim campaign reported run_79 sub-runs "failing the matching". The failures carried a scary-looking error — "a correlation IS present at −0.983 ms but ~2 µs wide … whatever DREAM was triggering on is only loosely associated with the n_TOF hits. Not slimmable." — the same signature previously used to write off 54 July sub-runs as a DAQ mystery.

That conclusion is retracted. The −0.98 ms feature was measured under healthy, successfully-fitting segments at the same lag and significance: it is the burst's own structure (the measured 0.9927 ms flash→first-physics-trigger hold-off edge cross-correlating with the candidate onset). It appears in failure logs purely by selection effect and carries no information about a segment.

The mechanism, precisely

The chain is two stages, both count-maximizing alignments against a quasi-periodic pulse train:

  1. pulse_match.match_subrun (per DREAM sub-run — which is why corruption is all-or-nothing per hour) scans a ±120 s offset against the beam-intensity record and keeps the offset matching the most clusters. Timing and the parasitic/dedicated intensity schedule both repeat with the supercycle, so locks one/two/ three cycles apart match ~100 % of clusters with ~5 ms rms — indistinguishable to the objective. On a tie, n > best_n keeps the first = most negative offset scanned; ±120 s admits exactly ±3 cycles, so failures sit at −3 supercycles (118.8 s at the 39.6 s schedule, 129.6 s at 43.2 s). Which hours fail is Poisson noise on which lock catches one more cluster.
  2. bunch_join's δ-scan (±3 s, per segment) inherits the wrong epoch and faithfully locks the corresponding integer bunch shift. The boundary slivers — the minority side of a sub-run straddling an n_TOF run restart — lost 26 of 26 straddling pairs in the campaign. (This was read as the same count-degeneracy against a truncated pulse list. It is not; it is the separate bootstrap defect below.)

A mis-locked segment looks perfectly healthy in every join statistic; it simply finds no coincidence, fails its clock fit, and writes no file. As the campaign session put it: "the QA is clean precisely because the broken ones are absent."

One integer at the join; zero changes to the fit chain. The recommended re-slim recipe for the 41 whole-hour failures: scan → apply → record provenance → standard chain (each scan gives a single unambiguous peak, demonstrated 8/8; ~one condor evening). The 66 sliver failures are a different bug, below.

Root cause 2 of 2: the sliver class was our own bootstrap

The section above blamed the slivers on the δ-scan, and an earlier version of this note blamed them on n_TOF. Both were wrong, and the reasoning failed in an instructive way.

dream_event_to_bunch bootstraps its final burst-to-pulse offset from the scan's lock:

delta = float(np.median(epoch - ps[assign(best_delta)]))      # WRONG

assign() returns the nearest pulse for every burst, clipped to the first or last pulse of the list. A burst whose pulse is not in this n_TOF run at all — every burst of the sub-run falling outside the run, which on a boundary sliver is the majority — still gets one, and contributes epoch − ps[0] instead of the offset. The median over all bursts therefore walks the offset by however far the sub-run overhangs the run. The docstring already said "the offset is DEFINED by the matched pairs"; the code never applied the mask.

run_79/stat090_0002 × 224573 (77 % overhang)value
δ-scan lock (correct)+0.790 s → 247 bursts, bunches 1–247
bursts with no pulse in this run806 of 1053 (77 %)
median over ALL bursts (shipped)−957.971 s
median over MATCHED only (correct)+0.837 s
what the corrupted δ produced277 bursts, bunches 1–527, resid 8 ms

That last row reproduces the shipped campaign log bit for bit. Every burst was paired with a pulse ~280 later than the one it belongs to.

Why it survived a whole campaign. Both sides sit on the 1.2 s PS grid, so a wrong lock is still a lock: residuals stayed at 8 ms and 277 of 277 bursts landed on the grid. And the check that was supposed to exonerate the bunch record — "recorded PulseIntensity matches the beam CSV at r = 1.0000" — was circular: it compares n_TOF against the CSV at the same index, and never compares DREAM against n_TOF. It would have returned 1.0000 no matter how wrong the mapping was.

How it was caught. Correlate every DREAM bunch against every n_TOF bunch of the run, then ask whether the best match sharpens to 20 ns bins — the signature of a real coincidence, which the envelope artifact never has. 129 of the 130 DREAM bunches whose partner exists in the file (99 %) are sharp at n_TOF bunch b−280: 45 counts in a 20 ns bin over a floor of zero, at a residual of −250 ns ± 20. The bunches whose partner would be numbered below 1 match nothing, exactly as they must. The n_TOF hits were never missing — they sat under a bunch index 280 lower than the one we asked for, which is why every earlier shift scan, bounded at ±200, swept past it.

The n_TOF side is clean, and that was measured rather than assumed. An earlier version of this note named an n_TOF per-bunch time-base anomaly as the open suspect. It should not have. Opening the failing run's files directly: the hit trees carry 200 bunches per partial in contiguous global numbering, the index tree carries the whole run's 3118 bunches, and the beam-pickup record holds 1000 bunches sitting exactly on the 1.2 s grid with zero unfilled timestamps and intensities identical to the index tree. Independently, our own reprocessing of the same raw data reproduced the failure exactly, which exonerates the processing recipe as well as the data. The one check that looked like it cleared the bunch mapping — recorded intensity against the beam CSV at r = 1.0000 — confirms only that n_TOF's record agrees with the accelerator's; being indexed the same way on both sides, it could never have detected our mapping error.

The fix, and the general guard. Mask the median to the matched pairs; then assert that the bootstrap has not moved the lock:

if abs(delta - best_delta) > PS_SPACING_S:   # 1.2 s
    raise RuntimeError(...)

The bootstrap refines a lock; it may not change it. Anything past one pulse spacing is a different lock arrived at silently — the shape this bug had, and the only reason it stayed invisible. Exemplar after the fix: 3954 σ, 247/247 bunches, 95.5598 % efficiency (cv 95.5206), accidental 0.0705 %, purity 99.9262 %. Regression where it must change nothing: 0.95895 vs 0.95895 shipped at full overlap, and 0.95898 vs 0.95898 at 24 % overhang — exact to five decimals.

It bites only when the overhang exceeds half the sub-run's bursts, which is when the median falls into the clipped population. That threshold was measured rather than assumed, by constructing segments at any overhang from one real segment's bursts and one real pulse list: it is sharp at 50 %, identical whether the sub-run overhangs at the start, the end or both, and the corruption grows continuously from zero as it is crossed — so there is no regime in which an over-threshold segment is quietly fine.

The fraction is of bursts, not of wall-clock time, and the two part company across a beam gap or a DAQ pause. Thinning the pre-run bursts while holding the sub-run's extent fixed leaves time-overhang pinned at 76.6 % while burst-overhang walks from 76.5 % to 29.1 % — and the corruption follows the bursts, crossing between 52.2 % and 45.1 %. So the overlap figures below, which come from the coverage map's wall clock, are a proxy: good where the beam is steady, wrong for precisely those segments that straddle a gap. Measured on the segment discussed below — 349 bursts in the sub-run, 232 matched by the n_TOF run, giving a 33.5 % burst overhang against a 61.4 % wall-clock one, because the beam ran at 12.3 bursts/min inside the run and 3.9/min over the overhanging stretch, 3.2× sparser.

So the proxy does not merely blur the classification — it can invert it. That segment is listed at 0.386 overlap, nominally deep in the region where the bug bites, and is actually at 0.665 in the units that matter: the other side of the line. Any segment straddling a beam gap can move that far, which is why the honest version of the table below is one computed in bursts by the corrected campaign, not a patch to this one.

The 18 failures above 0.5 are not explained by this bug — they are the first one. Crossing the 66 sliver failures against whether the same DREAM sub-run fitted on its other side (which pins its pulse_match offset): 17 of the 18 have no fitted sibling, the signature of a whole-sub-run supercycle mislock filed as a sliver merely because the sub-run straddles a run boundary. That is not correlation alone — two of the segments independently demonstrated to be supercycle mislocks, by cached offsets betraying a 118.8 s shift, sit in this list, as do both of the dark DREAM runs. They are covered by the first fix, not the second.

That left one unexplained segment: sibling-pinned, nominally 0.69 overlap so the bootstrap should not have reached it, yet it joined 44 bunches where it should have joined hundreds, with the "dropped pulses look like no beam" guard lit. It was tempting to call it a third mechanism. It was not — its overlap figure came from the same file-count duration extrapolation that produced the false alarm above, and on measured numbers it sits at 0.559 wall-clock and 0.691 burst overhang, over the threshold on both.

That was written down as a prediction before the job ran — bitten, therefore recovers — with the other side of the same sub-run as the control that validated the method. Observed: it recovers, at 94.715 % efficiency. The same job reproduced its neighbouring segment at 0.94480 against a shipped 0.94480, exact, at 0.242 burst overhang: the fix repairs the bitten end of the sub-run and leaves the well-behaved end untouched.

Every failure in the campaign is now accounted for by one of the two bugs. None is outstanding.

Pre-flight: five predictions registered in advance, five held

Before committing the full re-run, five segments were fixed one at a time — with each one's burst overhang computed and sent before its job ran, so the threshold could not be placed after the fact.

The 0.567 row is the load-bearing one: the threshold holds where it is thinnest. A sixth segment recovered that nobody predicted — run_79/0014 × 224577 at 94.64 %, the sub-run whose both halves failed originally, which had been offered at the outset as a 57-minute hole and as evidence that this whole class was an n_TOF problem. It was this bug.

Across the 23 comparable segments: 10 unchanged at an efficiency delta of +0.00000, 5 recovered, 8 refused pending a bunch-shift scan, and zero regressions. Ten exact reproductions in the same jobs as five recoveries is the discrimination that matters — a fix that merely joined more loosely would have moved both.

A false alarm worth recording

Between finding the bug and fixing it, one shipped product was accused of being silently wrong: a segment joining 232 bunches where its recorded 1.5-minute overlap, on a 1.2 s grid, caps at 75. The proposed gate — joined_bunches ≤ overlap_min·60/1.2 — was withdrawn, and the product is fine. overlap_min derives from a sub-run duration that is extrapolated from file count when no stop time is recorded, so the gate converts an estimator error into a data-quality verdict. The measurement that settles it was already in the product: 94.81 % of physics triggers matched at 0.052 % accidentals. A wrong-bunch join sits at the accidental rate — about 7×10−4 for ~1,000 candidates over a 75 ms burst — a factor ~1,400 below what that segment shows. The duration estimate was simply short.

Then it was measured rather than argued. That segment was re-run under the fixed code with a cold cache and came back at 0.94812 — identical to the shipped value to five decimals. The product was never corrupted, the efficiency instrument that defended it holds, and the claim that these bugs destroy data rather than corrupting it survives the one place where it was load-bearing for a specific shipped file. Nothing in the campaign's 170 products needs revisiting.

It also closes the last discrepancy. This segment sits at 61 % time overhang yet joins correctly, which under a threshold that is sharp at 50 % of bursts means its burst overhang must be below 50 %. Measured afterwards rather than left as an inference from the outcome: 33.5 %, from 232 of its 349 bursts falling inside the run. The beam really was thin over the overhanging stretch, by a factor of 3.2. The thinning table above is the mechanism; this is the observation that it happened.

The lesson generalises past this analysis: efficiency against the +100 µs control is the join-correctness instrument, and it is the same measurement as the b−280 ridge — a ±25 ns coincidence against a control. Any structural test built on a proposal, extrapolation or coverage estimate can produce a verdict about metadata, never about data.

The uncomfortable by-product: the 14

The margin study's fitted tail: 14 of the 170 accepted segments were decided by two clusters or fewer (two at margin exactly 0) — they pass every QA check and were a coin flip from the same failure. "170/170 passing QA" meant not shown wrong, not shown correct. They are listed for verification-by-scan alongside the 41 recoveries.

The fix (approved and implemented 08-12, commit ce8ced7)

  • pulse_match: score candidate locks by match count plus intensity-fluctuation correlation (the schedule repeats; the fluctuations don't — r 0.925 vs 0.508 picked the true lock outright in the wild) against the per-window grid measured from the pulse timestamps themselves; check offset continuity across a DREAM run's sub-runs; and fail loudly on an ambiguous winner. The silent tie-break return is the actual bug — everything else was symptom.
  • clock_qa gains an absolute check 'pulse_match margin adequate' (proposed WARN < 10, FAIL ≤ 2 unless scan-verified; the test set must include a margin-0-but-correct segment so the gate can't be tightened into rejecting good data).
  • Provenance before any bulk re-slim: calibration.json gains join_shift, lock margin and r-score, so recovered and originally-clean segments stay permanently distinguishable.

The kill-list

Twelve confident wrong models/numbers died to minutes-long measurements tonight. The sequence is the argument for the loud-failure requirement, and it reads better than a clean story taken on trust:

  1. "Not slimmable / DAQ mystery" (the Aug-9 conclusion) — the −0.982 ms basis fires on healthy data.
  2. Statistics floor in the coarse search — 14-min truncations fit easily.
  3. Bunch misassignment ±1 — flat shift scans.
  4. Noise-epoch flash mis-tag — no rate excess (+1.8 % where +40 % was needed).
  5. Missing flash trigger — forensics: the flash leads 100 % of corrupt bursts.
  6. Clean-bunch-fraction bridge — corruption is all-or-nothing per segment.
  7. Supercycle-in-pulse-counts — the period is in seconds; 26 pulses ≠ constant.
  8. Per-day schedule period — it changes between hours of one run.
  9. Schedule-based failure risk score — matched pair: identical schedule, opposite outcomes.
  10. "206 s, unexplained" — measured across the mislocked bunch range (bunch-index ≠ time).
  11. Four parser/classifier errors in campaign statistics (log-text parsing; summaries are the only truth).
  12. A period detector validated only where no ground truth existed (harmonic-picking comb).

Where everything lives

  • Campaign report: ntof_processing/SLIM_CAMPAIGN_2026-08-12.md (verdict, QA, exposure, mechanism, recipe, kill-list; regenerates from the tables).
  • Findings + analysis scripts: ntof_processing/join_mislock/ in the repo.
  • lxplus /afs/cern.ch/work/d/dneff/x17slim/: inventory.csv, shift_predictions.txt, margin_results.csv, all diag outputs, the recovery JSON.
  • Desktop /media/ucla/x17match/: self-contained sandbox (code + all data + scripts) for the sliver-class and run_86-quartet follow-ups.
  • Two incidental traps recorded on the way: consecutive BunchNumbers are n_TOF-recorded bunches, not PS pulses (bunch-index and wall-clock arithmetic diverge — only direct timestamp measurement is trustworthy); and PSTime in official merged files can be corrupt (denormals/NaN in run224607) — use Time.

Recovery scope: 41 whole-hour failures by plain re-run (demonstrated), plus the boundary-sliver population in the overhang region that 3a6c284 repairs, plus 17 mislocks-filed-as-slivers that the first fix already covers. That accounts for every failure in the campaign; none is outstanding. No recovery total is quoted here on purpose — the point of pre-flighting individual segments was to stop guessing, and the number comes from the full campaign when it measures it. A single campaign over all 83 runs from the fixed revision replaces the stopped one, so the products form one coherent set rather than two halves with different join semantics.

Status: ce8ced7 (pulse_match) and 3a6c284 (bunch_join) are committed; the re-slim campaign is pre-flighting three predicted recoveries before the full run. This note was corrected on 08-12 after the second root cause was found — the superseded claims are marked in place rather than deleted, since how the wrong ones survived is the more useful half of the record.
